title: Fabric Data Agent: Query-Generation Internals — Grounding, Per-Source Generators, and the Accuracy Levers
purpose: Show what happens between source selection and a generated query: which configuration surfaces ground the prompt, how the source-specific generator differs by data-source type, and which documented factors actually move answer accuracy.
accessibleSummary: An internals diagram. Four configuration surfaces — agent-level instructions, data-source-level instructions, data source descriptions, and up to 100 example queries per source — feed an assembled prompt sent to a managed Azure OpenAI Assistant alongside the user's question and the fetched schema. The assistant then routes to one of four source-specific generators: NL2SQL for lakehouse/warehouse, NL2DAX for Power BI semantic models, NL2KQL for Eventhouse KQL databases, or a Microsoft Graph/GQL query for ontology sources — each with its own quirks, most notably that Power BI semantic models do not support the example-query few-shot mechanism at all, and GQL generation against an ontology has three field-reported failure modes unrelated to SQL-based agents. A grounded accuracy-levers panel shows that community write-ups converge on instructions and data-model quality as the dominant lever, illustrated by a documented SCD2/bridge-table failure that disappeared once instructions were completed, the 'GINO' (Gold in Name Only) modeling antipattern that silently breaks NL2SQL agents, and a benchmark whose measured accuracy rose to about 97.2% after fixing both the benchmark's own ground truth and the agent's instructions. The output is a read-only, source-native query whose result is still subject to the 25×25 cap and governance precedence covered in the companion orchestration diagram.
longDescription: This diagram picks up exactly where the companion 'Life of a Fabric Data Agent Request' orchestration diagram leaves the query-generation step as a single box, and opens it up. It traces the four configuration surfaces a data-agent author actually sets — agent-level instructions (tenant-wide priorities and terminology, up to 15,000 characters), data-source-level instructions (scoped guidance that only applies once a source is already selected), data-source descriptions (the routing signal), and per-source example queries (a few-shot mechanism, up to 100 per source) — and shows how they combine with the user's question and the schema fetched under the caller's own identity into one assembled prompt for a managed Azure OpenAI Assistant. That assistant then hands off to a source-specific generator, and the diagram makes the differences between those four generators explicit rather than treating them as interchangeable: NL2SQL and NL2KQL both accept the example-query few-shot mechanism, NL2DAX for Power BI semantic models does not support it at all, and GQL generation against a Fabric IQ ontology carries three documented failure modes specific to graph structure. A closing panel names the factors community benchmarking converges on as the actual levers over answer accuracy — complete instructions and clean data modeling — rather than the underlying model.

nodes.label: Four configuration surfaces
nodes.summary: Agent instructions, source instructions, source descriptions, and example queries — the four levers an author actually sets.
nodes.detail: A Fabric data agent exposes four distinct configuration surfaces that together shape its behavior: agent-level instructions, data-source-level instructions, data source descriptions, and data-source example queries. Agent-level instructions operate above any single source and set overall objective, source priority order, key terminology, and response formatting, accepting up to 15,000 characters. Data-source-level instructions apply only once the agent has already routed a question to that specific source, holding source-specific guidance on relevant tables, columns, relationships, and query logic. A source description is a separate, high-level summary the agent uses as a routing signal. Example queries pair sample questions with validated SQL or KQL as a few-shot mechanism, up to 100 per attached source.
nodes.whyItMatters: These four surfaces are the only inputs an author directly controls. Getting them right or leaving them thin is, per the accuracy-levers panel later in this diagram, the single biggest documented factor in whether the agent answers correctly.

evidence.note: A Fabric data agent exposes four distinct configuration surfaces that together shape its behavior: agent-level instructions, data-source-level instructions, data source descriptions, and data-source example queries.

Agent-level instructions operate above any single data source and are meant to state the agent's overall objective, set a priority order across attached data sources, define key terminology/acronyms, and specify response-formatting expectations.

Agent-level instructions accept up to 15,000 characters of plain-English guidance and can direct the agent to prefer specific sources for specific question types or define domain-specific terminology the model otherwise misinterprets.

Data-source-level instructions apply only once the agent has already routed a question to a specific source, and are meant to hold source-specific guidance such as relevant tables, columns, relationships, and query logic needed for common or complex questions.

A data source description is a separate, high-level summary of what a given attached source contains and what kinds of questions it can answer, and the agent uses this description as one of its inputs when deciding which source is relevant to a given user question.

inputs: Attached source schemas and business terminology
Prior support/diagnostics feedback on wrong answers
processing: Author writes agent-level instructions: objective, source priority order, glossary of acronyms, response-format rules
Author writes per-source instructions: which tables/columns/relationships matter, source-specific query logic
Author writes a one-line description per source so the router can match it to likely questions
Author (optionally) supplies up to 100 example question/query pairs per source, syntax- and schema-validated
outputs: A grounded, source-scoped configuration the runtime reads at query time — never bundled into one flat prompt blob
drill.example: An agent over a sales lakehouse sets agent-level instructions defining 'active customer' once, then per-source instructions on the lakehouse pointing at the correct fact/dimension join keys, plus three example queries showing how to compute trailing-12-month revenue correctly.
controls: Recommended agent-level template: Objective, Data sources, Key terminology, Response guidelines, Handling common topics
Recommended source-level template: General knowledge, Table descriptions, When asked about
Git integration to version-control instructions and example queries
Deployment pipelines to promote a tuned configuration dev → prod
failureModes: Leaving instructions default/empty and expecting the model to infer business meaning from column names alone
Writing agent-level guidance that duplicates or contradicts source-level guidance

nodes.label: Example queries (few-shot)
nodes.summary: Top-3 relevant examples are looked up per source and passed into generation — except Power BI semantic models, which don't support this at all.
nodes.detail: Example queries function as few-shot learning: creators pair sample questions with validated SQL or KQL, and the agent matches new questions against these to steer generation toward business-specific logic. When a data source is selected, its tool automatically looks up the most relevant example queries and passes the top three into the query-generation step. Only syntactically valid, schema-matching examples are ever used. Power BI semantic models do not support this example-query mechanism at all.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the sharpest per-source-type asymmetry in the whole pipeline: two of the four generator paths get a documented accuracy lever that one of them structurally cannot use, which is a real design constraint, not an oversight to route around.

evidence.note: Example queries function as few-shot learning: creators pair sample questions with validated SQL or KQL, and the agent matches new questions against these to steer generation toward business-specific logic; only syntactically valid, schema-matching examples are ever used, and Power BI semantic models don't support this example-query mechanism.

Data source example queries are a few-shot mechanism: when a data source is selected for a question, its tool automatically looks up the most relevant example queries and passes the top three into the query-generation step.

processing: Source's example-query tool ranks stored examples by relevance to the current question
Top three are selected
Selected examples are passed alongside schema into the assembled prompt
outputs: Up to three validated question/query pairs steering the generator toward business-specific phrasing
drill.example: A warehouse source has 40 stored example queries; for a question about quarterly churn, the three examples closest to 'churn' and 'quarter' phrasing are surfaced to the generator, not the full 40.
controls: Up to 100 example queries per attached source
Only syntactically valid, schema-matching examples are ever stored/used
failureModes: Assuming a Power BI semantic model source benefits from example queries the same way a lakehouse does — it structurally does not

nodes.label: Assembled prompt
nodes.summary: Question, fetched schema, and creator instructions/examples are assembled into one prompt before a generator is chosen.
nodes.detail: The prompt sent to the underlying Azure OpenAI Assistant is assembled from three inputs: the user's natural-language question, the fetched schema metadata, and any creator-supplied instructions or example queries, before the assistant selects a query-generation tool.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the single point where all grounding — question, schema, and every configuration surface — converges before the model decides how to answer. Weak input anywhere upstream degrades everything downstream of this node.

evidence.note: The prompt sent to the underlying Azure OpenAI Assistant is assembled from three inputs: the user's natural-language question, the fetched schema metadata, and any creator-supplied instructions or example queries, before the assistant selects a query-generation tool.

When answering a question, the agent first fetches the target data source's schema using the requesting user's own credentials, guaranteeing schema visibility is scoped to what that user can already see.

inputs: Schema metadata fetched under the caller's identity
processing: Three input categories merged into one prompt
Prompt handed to a Microsoft-managed Azure OpenAI Assistant
Assistant selects which source-specific generation tool to invoke
outputs: One assembled, source-scoped prompt ready for source-specific query generation
drill.example: For a KQL-database question, the assembled prompt contains the question, the relevant table/column schema the caller can see, and any source-level instructions about time-filtering conventions for that Eventhouse.
controls: What goes into instructions and example queries is fully author-controlled; schema and question are not
failureModes: Schema fetch scoped to the caller means two different users asking the identical question can get differently-grounded prompts if their visible schema differs (e.g. column-level security)

nodes.label: NL2SQL (lakehouse / warehouse)
nodes.summary: Generates read-only SQL against lakehouse and warehouse sources.
nodes.detail: After identifying the relevant data source, the agent routes the question to a source-specific generator: NL2SQL for lakehouse/warehouse, NL2DAX for Power BI semantic models, NL2KQL for KQL databases, or a Microsoft Graph query for organizational data. NL2SQL is the path used for lakehouse and warehouse sources.
nodes.whyItMatters: SQL generation quality is directly downstream of how clean the underlying gold-layer modeling is — a superficially-relabeled bronze table (see the GINO antipattern node) breaks this generator silently rather than loudly.

evidence.note: After identifying the relevant data source, the agent routes the question to a source-specific generator: NL2SQL for lakehouse/warehouse, NL2DAX for Power BI semantic models, NL2KQL for KQL databases, or a Microsoft Graph query for organizational data.

processing: Generator drafts a read-only SELECT statement against the source's SQL surface
Statement is scoped to tables/columns the schema fetch exposed
outputs: A read-only SQL query, never a write statement
drill.example: 'What were total sales by region last quarter?' against a warehouse source generates a SELECT with a GROUP BY region and a date filter matching the prior quarter.
controls: Table descriptions and column-level guidance in source-level instructions
Example SQL queries as few-shot grounding
failureModes: Multi-grain fact tables or unnecessary normalization (the GINO antipattern) silently produce wrong joins/aggregations that a human analyst would catch but the generator does not

nodes.label: NL2DAX (semantic model)
nodes.summary: Generates DAX against Power BI semantic models; Read permission is enough, but no example-query few-shot is available.
nodes.detail: NL2DAX is the generator path used for Power BI semantic model sources. Only Read permission on the model is required for the agent to retrieve schema and run queries — Build permission is not needed — though Row-Level and Column-Level Security still apply. This is also the one source type where the example-query few-shot mechanism is unsupported.
nodes.whyItMatters: Semantic models are the only source type in this diagram both permission-relaxed (Read-only suffices) and few-shot-deprived (no example queries), a distinctive combination worth designing an agent's instructions around.

evidence.note: After identifying the relevant data source, the agent routes the question to a source-specific generator: NL2SQL for lakehouse/warehouse, NL2DAX for Power BI semantic models, NL2KQL for KQL databases, or a Microsoft Graph query for organizational data.

For Power BI semantic model sources, only Read permission on the model is required for the agent to retrieve schema and run queries; Build permission is not needed, though Row-Level and Column-Level Security still apply.

Example queries function as few-shot learning: creators pair sample questions with validated SQL or KQL, and the agent matches new questions against these to steer generation toward business-specific logic; only syntactically valid, schema-matching examples are ever used, and Power BI semantic models don't support this example-query mechanism.

inputs: Semantic model schema (tables, measures, relationships) visible under Read permission
No example-query few-shot — unsupported for this source type
processing: Generator drafts a DAX query against the model's measures and columns
RLS/CLS on the model is evaluated as part of execution, not generation
outputs: A DAX query scoped to what the model's certified measures expose
drill.example: 'What's our year-over-year revenue growth?' resolves to a DAX query calling the model's existing YoY-growth measure rather than reconstructing the calculation from raw columns.
controls: Agent- and source-level instructions are the only few-shot-equivalent lever available for this source type, since example queries don't apply
Endorsed/certified measures narrow what the generator needs to reconstruct
failureModes: Because there's no example-query mechanism here, ambiguous or undocumented measure names are more likely to be misused than on SQL-based sources

nodes.label: NL2KQL (Eventhouse)
nodes.summary: Generates KQL against Eventhouse KQL databases, queried in place with no data movement.
nodes.detail: NL2KQL is the generator path used for KQL databases. Eventhouse KQL databases are queried in place by the agent with no data movement, and NL2KQL can use existing KQL user-defined functions; configurators are advised to scope to the most relevant tables and encourage time filters to keep responses fast over high-volume event data.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the one generator with an explicit performance-shaping recommendation baked into its own documentation — time-filter guidance — because the underlying data volume (streaming event data) is structurally larger than a typical lakehouse table scan.

evidence.note: After identifying the relevant data source, the agent routes the question to a source-specific generator: NL2SQL for lakehouse/warehouse, NL2DAX for Power BI semantic models, NL2KQL for KQL databases, or a Microsoft Graph query for organizational data.

Eventhouse KQL databases are queried in place by the agent with no data movement, and NL2KQL can use existing KQL user-defined functions; configurators are advised to scope to the most relevant tables and encourage time filters to keep responses fast over high-volume event data.

inputs: KQL database schema and existing user-defined functions
processing: Generator drafts a KQL query, optionally reusing existing KQL UDFs and materialized views
Query executes directly against the Eventhouse, no copy or staging step
outputs: A read-only KQL query scoped to the most relevant tables
drill.example: 'How many device errors in the last hour?' generates a KQL query with a `where Timestamp > ago(1h)` filter, matching the documented advice to encourage time filters over high-volume event tables.
controls: Source-level instructions can point the generator at existing KQL UDFs instead of hand-writing logic
Scoping instructions to the most relevant tables keeps generated queries fast over high-volume data
failureModes: A question with no natural time bound can generate a KQL query that scans a much larger window of event data than intended

nodes.label: Graph / GQL (ontology)
nodes.summary: Generates a Microsoft Graph or GQL query for ontology sources — three documented failure modes distinct from SQL-based generators.
nodes.detail: After identifying the relevant data source, the agent can also route a question to a Microsoft Graph query for organizational data or a graph-backed ontology. A field report on building a data agent against a graph-backed ontology found practical failure modes distinct from SQL-based agents: asynchronous graph rebuild timing, the need to use binding property names rather than display names in generated GQL, and a hidden requirement to prefix SQL objects with `dbo.` that the agent otherwise omits.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the least SQL-like generator in the set, and its documented failure modes don't transfer from anything learned tuning the other three — it needs its own configuration playbook.

evidence.note: After identifying the relevant data source, the agent routes the question to a source-specific generator: NL2SQL for lakehouse/warehouse, NL2DAX for Power BI semantic models, NL2KQL for KQL databases, or a Microsoft Graph query for organizational data.

One field report on building a Fabric Data Agent against a graph-backed ontology (GQL) found practical failure modes distinct from SQL-based agents: asynchronous graph rebuild timing, the need to use binding property names rather than display names in generated GQL, and a hidden requirement to prefix SQL objects with dbo. that the agent otherwise omits.

inputs: Instance graph state, which may lag an upstream data change
processing: Generator drafts a GQL query against the ontology's published entity types and relationships
Query is constrained to what the ontology has explicitly modeled, not raw source schema
outputs: A structured graph query answer, grounded in the shared ontology's definitions
drill.example: A field report describes generated GQL failing until property references were switched from human-readable display names to the ontology's internal binding property names.
controls: Awareness that the instance graph rebuilds asynchronously, so a very recent source change may not yet be reflected
Explicit binding-name usage in source/agent instructions for ontology sources
failureModes: Asynchronous graph rebuild timing means a question can be answered against a stale instance graph
Using display names instead of binding property names in generated GQL
Omitting a required `dbo.` prefix on underlying SQL objects that the agent doesn't add automatically

nodes.label: What actually moves accuracy
nodes.summary: Community benchmarking converges: instructions and data-model quality are the dominant lever, not the underlying model.
nodes.detail: Multiple independent community write-ups converge on the same conclusion: agent instructions and data-model documentation are the biggest lever for answer accuracy, with one side-by-side demo showing a minimally-instructed agent silently returning wrong answers on complex SCD2/bridge-table queries while an identically-sourced agent with full instructions answered correctly. A separate community-built, Spider2-inspired 72-question multilingual benchmark initially showed weaker accuracy, but a row-level audit found many failures traced to faulty ground truth, ambiguous phrasing, and inconsistent casing in the benchmark itself; after fixing the benchmark and tightening agent instructions, measured accuracy rose to about 97.2%.
nodes.whyItMatters: This reframes 'the agent got it wrong' as usually a configuration and modeling problem, not a model-capability problem — the fix is almost always upstream in this diagram (instructions, schema quality), not in generator internals.

evidence.note: Multiple independent community write-ups converge on the same conclusion: agent instructions and data-model documentation are the biggest lever for answer accuracy, with one side-by-side demo showing a minimally-instructed agent silently returning wrong answers on complex SCD2/bridge-table queries while an identically-sourced agent with full instructions answered correctly.

A community-built, Spider2-inspired 72-question multilingual benchmark evaluated with the Fabric evaluate_data_agent SDK function initially showed weaker accuracy, but a row-level audit found many failures traced back to faulty ground truth, ambiguous phrasing, and inconsistent casing in the benchmark itself rather than agent mistakes; after fixing the benchmark and tightening agent instructions, measured accuracy rose to about 97.2%, with remaining errors attributed to complex multi-step prompts and ambiguous schema references.

inputs: Baseline agent with minimal or default instructions
Complex query patterns (SCD2, bridge tables, multi-step questions)
processing: Compare minimally-instructed vs fully-instructed agent on the same source and question set
Audit benchmark failures row-by-row to separate agent errors from ground-truth errors
Fix benchmark ground truth and tighten agent instructions
Re-measure
outputs: A measured accuracy improvement attributable mostly to instructions and modeling quality, not model swaps
drill.example: A side-by-side demo: the same underlying source and model, one agent with empty instructions and one with completed instructions, diverged sharply on SCD2/bridge-table questions — only the instructed agent answered correctly.
controls: Completing all four configuration surfaces before blaming generator accuracy
Fixing gold-layer modeling quality (avoiding the GINO antipattern) before tuning instructions further
failureModes: Treating a wrong answer as a model-capability limitation when it traces back to thin instructions or messy modeling
Trusting a benchmark's own ground truth without auditing it, as the Spider2-inspired benchmark's own creators had to do

nodes.label: Warning: "GINO" — Gold in Name Only
nodes.summary: A gold layer that's only superficially relabeled bronze silently breaks NL2SQL agents.
nodes.detail: A community article coined the term 'GINO' (Gold in Name Only) for a data-modeling antipattern where a bronze-quality dataset is superficially relabeled as a Gold layer while still containing multi-grain fact tables, unnecessarily normalized structures, and outer joins. The author argues this antipattern, which a human analyst can work around, silently breaks NL2SQL agents, and proposes simplifying toward Kimball-style star schemas as the fix.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the concrete, sourced mechanism behind the general 'data modeling matters for accuracy' claim — it names the exact antipattern and the exact generator it damages (NL2SQL), and gives a specific fix.

evidence.note: A community article coined the term 'GINO' (Gold in Name Only) for a data-modeling antipattern where a bronze-quality dataset is superficially relabeled as a Gold layer while still containing multi-grain fact tables, unnecessarily normalized structures, and outer joins; the author argues this antipattern that a human analyst can work around silently breaks NL2SQL agents, and proposes simplifying toward Kimball-style star schemas as the fix.

inputs: A 'gold' layer table that is really bronze-quality: multi-grain facts, unnecessary normalization, outer joins
processing: NL2SQL generator infers joins and aggregation grain from schema alone
Ambiguous grain or normalization leads to a plausible-looking but wrong query
No error is raised — the query executes and returns a confidently wrong answer
outputs: A silently incorrect SQL query and answer, indistinguishable from a correct one without independent verification
drill.example: A fact table mixing order-line grain and order-header grain in one table produces a NL2SQL-generated SUM that double-counts header-level fields when joined naively, with no error surfaced.
controls: Simplify toward Kimball-style star schemas before exposing a table to a data agent
Table descriptions and source-level instructions can partially compensate, but do not fix the underlying grain ambiguity
failureModes: Relabeling bronze tables as 'gold' without actually remodeling them
Trusting a data agent's SQL output on a table a human analyst already has to work around manually

nodes.label: Read-only query + governed answer
nodes.summary: Every generator hands back a read-only, source-native query; the result is still capped and governance-gated downstream.
nodes.detail: The agent enforces read-only, least-privilege access by executing under the requesting user's own credentials and permissions, so each query only reaches data that user is already authorized to view. Agent responses are capped at a maximum of 25 rows and 25 columns. Agent behavior is governed by a four-layer precedence model — tenant policy, workspace governance, developer instructions, end-user prompt — evaluated before the answer is returned.
nodes.whyItMatters: Regardless of which of the four generators produced the query, execution and answer shaping converge on the same identity-scoped, capped, governance-gated path — the generator choice only changes how the query was written, not what it's allowed to return.

evidence.note: The agent enforces read-only, least-privilege access by executing under the requesting user's own credentials and permissions, so each query only reaches data that user is already authorized to view.

Agent responses are capped at a maximum of 25 rows and 25 columns, and because prior chat turns can influence later answers, a request like asking for all rows for a year will still be limited to 25 rows even in follow-up questions within the same session.

Agent behavior is governed by a four-layer precedence model, from highest to lowest: tenant-wide organizational policy, workspace/role-based governance settings, developer-supplied instructions and example queries, and finally end-user prompts; higher layers always override lower ones.

inputs: A generated read-only query from any of the four source-specific generators
processing: Query executes under the caller's own identity and permissions
Four-layer governance precedence is applied
Result truncated to 25 rows × 25 columns
outputs: A capped, permission-scoped, query-transparent answer — see the companion orchestration diagram for the full request lifecycle including failure branches
drill.example: Two users asking the same question against the same semantic model can get different results if their Row-Level Security assignments differ, even though the generated DAX query is identical.
controls: This node deliberately does not re-derive the full orchestration/failure-branch detail already covered in the companion diagram
failureModes: Assuming a generator-specific optimization (e.g. KQL time filters) removes the need for the 25×25 cap downstream — it does not
